claims.text: An explainable machine-learning model trained on high-fidelity simulations and experimental data can accurately predict unusually low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
The model would work by capturing nonlinear correlations involving mass disorder, chemical-bond fluctuations, and anharmonicity.
The proposed model would outperform traditional lattice-dynamics and empirical models.
High-entropy alloys used in the proposed application have disordered, multielement configurations with substantial point disorder and chemical inhomogeneity.
Ab initio molecular dynamics can be used to train machine-learned force fields that are subsequently combined with Green–Kubo calculations of thermal conductivity.
Phonon scattering dominates heat transport from room temperature to the proposed elevated-temperature range.
The approach is intended for alloys with more than five principal elements that are well represented in the training data.
Multielement mixing produces point disorder and local chemical-bond fluctuations.
Mass, strain-field, and force-constant fluctuations contribute to phonon scattering in compositionally disordered materials.
Electronegativity differences increase chemical-bond complexity and can contribute to lattice thermal conductivity.
The model will learn relationships between compositional descriptors and the resulting phonon-scattering effects.
The learned relationships will enable identification of alloys with lattice thermal conductivity below 1 W/(m·K).
The model will reduce prediction error by more than 20% relative to traditional physics-based or empirical models.
Traditional lattice-dynamics and empirical correlations oversimplify phonon scattering in disordered multielement alloys and consequently have higher prediction errors.
Predictive reliability is limited to composition and temperature domains similar to those represented in the training data.
Predictions may be less reliable for extreme compositions and temperatures at which nonphonon heat-transport mechanisms dominate.
Existing high-entropy-alloy datasets are limited and biased, creating uncertainty and extrapolation risk.
Strong anharmonicity, reflected by large Grüneisen parameters, can be associated with very low thermal conductivity.
The benchmark will compare model predictions against measured lattice thermal conductivity from room temperature to 500 K and against traditional-model errors.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least 20%, or failure to identify alloys below 1 W/(m·K), will falsify the hypothesis.
